title: Microscopic Electric Conduction, Drift Velocity, and Carrier Mobility
learning_objective: Explain the microscopic mechanism of metallic conduction, relate the drift velocity of charge carriers to an applied electric field through carrier mobility, and formulate current density as a charge flux.
explanation:
In metallic conductors, valence electrons become delocalized, forming a dense electron gas with number density $n \sim 10^{28}-10^{29}\,\text{m}^{-3}$. In the absence of an external electric field, these conduction electrons undergo chaotic thermal motion, bouncing off vibrating lattice ions at Fermi/thermal speeds $v_{\text{thermal}} \sim 10^5-10^6\,\text{m/s}$. Because the thermal velocities are isotropically distributed in all directions, the time-averaged vector velocity across the electron ensemble is identically zero: $\langle \vec{v}_{\text{thermal}} \rangle = \vec{0}$, yielding zero net macroscopic electric current.

When an external electric field $\vec{E}$ is established inside the conductor (for instance, by connecting a potential difference across its terminals), each electron experiences an electrostatic force $\vec{F} = -e\vec{E}$, resulting in an acceleration $\vec{a} = -\frac{e\vec{E}}{m}$. Between successive collisions with lattice ions, an electron accelerates in the direction opposite to $\vec{E}$. Each collision rapidly randomizes the electron's momentum. Over a statistical mean relaxation time $\tau$ (typically $\sim 10^{-14}\,\text{s}$ at room temperature), the electrons acquire a net steady average velocity termed the drift velocity $\vec{v}_d$:
$$\vec{v}_d = \vec{a}\tau = -\frac{e\tau}{m}\vec{E}$$
The magnitude of drift speed per unit electric field defines the electron mobility $\mu$:
$$\mu = \frac{v_d}{E} = \frac{e\tau}{m}$$

To connect this microscopic drift to macroscopic current $I$, consider a conductor of cross-sectional area $A$. In a small time interval $\Delta t$, the mobile electrons drift through an average axial distance $\Delta x = v_d\Delta t$. The total mobile charge contained within the corresponding cylindrical volume element $\Delta V = A\Delta x = A v_d\Delta t$ crossing the section is $\Delta q = (n \Delta V) e = n e A v_d \Delta t$. Taking the time derivative yields the fundamental transport equation:
$$I = \frac{\Delta q}{\Delta t} = n e A v_d$$

The current density vector $\vec{J}$ is the electric current flowing per unit cross-sectional area normal to the charge flow: $\vec{J} = \frac{I}{A}\hat{n} = n q \vec{v}_d = -n e \vec{v}_d$. Substituting $\vec{v}_d = -\frac{e\tau}{m}\vec{E}$ yields the microscopic form of Ohm's Law:
$$\vec{J} = \left(\frac{n e^2\tau}{m}\right)\vec{E} = \sigma \vec{E}$$
where $\sigma = \frac{n e^2\tau}{m}$ is the electrical conductivity of the conductor (with SI units $\Omega^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-1}$ or $\text{S/m}$), and its reciprocal $\rho = \frac{1}{\sigma} = \frac{m}{n e^2\tau}$ is the electrical resistivity (in $\Omega\,\text{m}$).

A vital conceptual point in electrodynamics is the stark contrast between the drift speed $v_d$ and the signal propagation speed. While $v_d$ is remarkably sluggish—typically on the order of $10^{-4}\,\text{m/s}$ or a fraction of a millimeter per second—an electric circuit turns on virtually instantaneously when switched on because the electric field propagates through the conductor via electromagnetic waves at nearly the speed of light ($c \sim 3 \times 10^8\,\text{m/s}$).
intuition: Imagine a dense crowd of thousands of people packed tightly into a long corridor, all sprinting chaotically in random directions at meters per second, constantly bumping into one another so that the crowd as a whole remains stationary. If someone gently tilts the entire corridor downhill, every person still bounces frantically back and forth at high speed, but the whole crowd collectively crawls downhill at a few millimeters per minute. The frantic bouncing is the electron thermal motion ($10^5\,\text{m/s}$), the downhill slope is the applied electric field $\vec{E}$, and the slow collective crawl is the drift velocity ($10^{-4}\,\text{m/s}$).
formal_definition: Drift velocity $\vec{v}_d$ is the ensemble-averaged vector velocity acquired by free charge carriers in a conductive medium under the influence of an applied macroscopic electric field $\vec{E}$, governed by $\vec{v}_d = -\mu \vec{E} = -\frac{e\tau}{m}\vec{E}$, where $\mu$ is carrier mobility, $e$ is elementary charge, $m$ is effective carrier mass, and $\tau$ is momentum relaxation time.
assumptions: Classical Drude model of non-interacting free electron gas in an isotropic ionic lattice
Independent electron collisions that completely randomize velocity with mean relaxation time $\tau$
Uniform electric field $\vec{E}$ throughout the cross-section of the conductor
Steady-state DC current with negligible inductive or capacitive transient effects
boundary_conditions: Valid for linear ohmic metals where drift speed is negligible compared to thermal Fermi velocity ($v_d \ll v_{\text{thermal}}$)
Invalid in ballistic conductors where sample dimensions are smaller than electron mean free path
Invalid under extreme electric fields where carrier heating induces non-linear velocity saturation
